concept.name: Fenwick Trees (Binary Indexed Trees)

relationships.description: Connects Fenwick Trees (Binary Indexed Trees) to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A 1-indexed array that maintains dynamic prefix sums and point updates in O(log N) time using two's complement bit isolation (`i & -i`), requiring zero pointer overhead and half the memory of a segment tree.
spark.keyTakeaway: When you need fast cumulative sums over a mutable array, isolating the lowest set bit with `i & -i` lets a flat array act as an implicit binary tree in L1/L2 cache.

concept.whyItMatters: Naive prefix-sum arrays answer range queries in O(1) time but require O(N) to rebuild on every update, while naive mutable arrays update in O(1) but scan O(N) per sum. A Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) bridges both operations at O(log N) using a single contiguous primitive array, making it a staple in limit order books, entropy coders, and streaming quantile trackers.
whenToUse: You maintain a fixed-size mutable frequency or weight array of size N where both point updates and prefix/range sum queries occur at high frequency (e.g., >100k ops/sec).
Memory footprint and CPU cache locality are critical—a Fenwick Tree stores N+1 primitives (e.g., 512 KB for 65,536 `int64` entries) versus 2N–4N nodes for a segment tree.
You need O(log N) order-statistic queries (`findKthSmallest`) via binary lifting over cumulative frequency counts without maintaining a balanced BST.
whenNotToUse: Your range query is non-invertible, such as `min`, `max`, or `gcd`—Fenwick Trees rely on `rangeSum(l, r) = prefix(r) - prefix(l - 1)`, which fails without an inverse operation.
The index space is sparse and massive (e.g., 64-bit timestamps or arbitrary strings) without coordinate compression, as allocating an array of size U wastes gigabytes.
Updates are predominantly range-assign or complex lazy-propagation operations across arbitrary intervals, where a segment tree is cleaner and avoids dual-BIT tricks.
keyPoints: Every index `i` (1-based) in `tree[1..N]` stores the sum of a subrange of length `LSB(i) = i & -i` ending at `i`, specifically `[i - (i & -i) + 1, i]`.
Point updates (`add(i, delta)`) climb responsibility ranges upward via `i += i & -i` until `i > N`, touching at most `floor(log2(N)) + 1` elements.
Prefix queries (`sum(i)`) accumulate disjoint segments downward via `i -= i & -i` until `i == 0`, summing at most `popcount(i)` elements.
Linear-time O(N) construction is possible in a single pass by propagating `tree[i]` to its immediate parent `j = i + (i & -i)` if `j <= N`, beating O(N log N) repeated inserts.
Binary lifting finds the smallest index with `prefixSum(idx) >= k` in a single O(log N) pass by testing powers of two from `2^floor(log2(N))` down to `1`.

examples.title: Limit Order Book Cumulative Depth
examples.scenario: A matching engine tracks Resting Bid Volume across 65,536 discrete price ticks (`N = 2^16`). Market-data consumers repeatedly query total volume within 50 ticks of the best bid while order cancellations and fills mutate individual ticks.
examples.outcome: Storing `int64` volumes in a 512 KB Fenwick Tree fits comfortably in L2 cache. Point updates and range depth queries each execute at most 16 loop iterations (~35–50 ns in C++/Rust), avoiding pointer chasing and GC pressure.

examples.title: Adaptive Arithmetic Coding Frequency Table
examples.scenario: An entropy encoder (similar to range coding in LZMA/Zstandard variants) maps 256–4,096 symbol frequencies to cumulative probability intervals `[low, high)` and increments each symbol's count after encoding it.
examples.outcome: A Fenwick Tree computes `[cumFreq(s-1), cumFreq(s))` and updates `freq[s]` in <=12 bit-masked additions, keeping symbol lookup and model adaptation O(log |Sigma|) instead of O(|Sigma|).

tradeOffs.pro: Uses exactly `N + 1` contiguous primitives with zero child pointers, achieving ~2–4x better cache hit rates than pointer-based trees.
tradeOffs.con: Restricted strictly to invertible associative operations (addition, XOR, modular arithmetic); cannot natively compute range minimum/maximum.

tradeOffs.pro: Combining two Fenwick Trees (`B1` and `B2`) supports O(log N) range-add and range-sum queries while preserving flat array layout.
tradeOffs.con: Doubles array memory and requires maintaining `sum(i) = i * query(B1, i) - query(B2, i)`, increasing overflow risk and code complexity.

tradeOffs.factor: Static Allocation vs. Dynamic Key Spaces
tradeOffs.pro: Pre-allocating `tree[N+1]` guarantees deterministic latency with zero heap allocations during hot-path updates.
tradeOffs.con: Requires known upper bound `N` upfront or offline coordinate compression; resizing requires an O(N) reallocation and rebuild.

failureModes.name: Zero-Index Infinite Loop
failureModes.description: Passing `i = 0` into an update loop `while (i <= N) { tree[i] += delta; i += i & -i; }` causes `0 & -0 == 0`, hanging the thread forever.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict 1-based indexing at the public API boundary (`idx + 1` internally) and assert `i >= 1` before entering bit-manipulation loops.

failureModes.name: 32-bit Integer Overflow on Prefix Accumulation
failureModes.description: Individual deltas fit in `int32`, but cumulative sums across `N = 10^6` elements exceed `2^31 - 1`, silently wrapping negative.
failureModes.mitigation: Store tree nodes as `int64` (or `uint64`) whenever `N * max_abs_delta` can exceed `2^31 - 1`, especially in dual-BIT range-update setups where `i * query(B1, i)` scales by `N`.

failureModes.name: Non-Invertible Monoid Misuse
failureModes.description: Attempting `rangeMax(l, r) = prefixMax(r) - prefixMax(l - 1)` or assuming BIT `query(r)` returns a range minimum produces corrupted results.
failureModes.mitigation: Verify the operation forms an abelian group (has an inverse) before choosing a Fenwick Tree; switch to a Segment Tree or Sparse Table for `min`/`max`/`gcd`.

failureModes.name: Torn Reads Under Concurrent Mutation
failureModes.description: A reader traversing `i -= i & -i` concurrently with a writer climbing `i += i & -i` observes partially propagated deltas, yielding impossible negative or inconsistent range sums.
failureModes.mitigation: Protect updates and reads with a single-writer lock, use partitioned per-thread trees merged at read time, or swap immutable snapshots for read-heavy workloads.

commonMistakes: Allocating `new long[N]` instead of `new long[N + 1]`, triggering an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when updating index `N`.
Using `rangeSum(l, r) = sum(r) - sum(l)` instead of `sum(r) - sum(l - 1)`, which drops the element at index `l`.
Forgetting to scale `N` to the compressed coordinate count rather than raw input values.
Implementing `findKthSmallest` by binary-searching `sum(mid)` in O(log^2 N) instead of O(log N) binary lifting.
Using `i & (~i + 1)` on unsigned types in languages without careful casting, or assuming right-shift behavior matches signed two's complement.

sections.content:
## The idea

Every positive integer `i` has a unique binary representation, which means any prefix `[1, i]` can be partitioned into disjoint power-of-two blocks corresponding to the set bits of `i`. For example, `i = 13` (`1101` in binary) splits `[1, 13]` into `[1, 8]` (length 8), `[9, 12]` (length 4), and `[13, 13]` (length 1). A Fenwick Tree stores each block's sum at its right endpoint: `tree[i]` holds the sum of the last `i & -i` elements ending at `i`.

Because `i & -i` isolates the lowest set bit in a single CPU cycle (`BLSI` on x86-64 BMI1), stripping that bit (`i -= i & -i`) walks through the exact disjoint blocks of `[1, i]` during a query. Conversely, adding the lowest set bit (`i += i & -i`) jumps to the smallest enclosing block that also covers index `i` during an update.

sections.content:
## Binary lifting and O(N) initialization

Two optimizations separate production Fenwick Trees from textbook versions. First, **O(N) construction** avoids `N` calls to `add()`: copy initial values into `tree[1..N]`, then iterate `i` from `1` to `N`, computing `parent = i + (i & -i)` and executing `if (parent <= N) tree[parent] += tree[i]`. Every node adds its finalized subtree sum to its immediate parent once.

Second, **binary lifting** finds the smallest index `idx` with `prefixSum(idx) >= k` in O(log N) rather than O(log^2 N). Starting from `bit = highestPowerOfTwo(N)` down to `1`, test `next = pos + bit`. If `next <= N` and `sum + tree[next] < k`, commit `pos = next` and `sum += tree[next]`. Because `tree[pos + bit]` already aggregates `[pos + 1, pos + bit]`, each step takes O(1) work.

## Data structure comparison

| Metric | Fenwick Tree (BIT) | Iterative Segment Tree | Sorted Balanced BST (Treap/RB) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Space** | `N + 1` words | `2N` words | `~4N–6N` words + pointers |
| **Point Update** | `O(log N)` (~16 ops @ 64K) | `O(log N)` | `O(log N)` + rotations |
| **Range Sum** | `O(log N)` | `O(log N)` | `O(log N)` |
| **Range Min/Max** | Unsupported | `O(log N)` | `O(log N)` |
| **Cache Locality** | High (flat array, low stride) | Medium-High | Poor (heap pointer chasing) |
| **Dynamic Key Space** | Needs compression | Needs compression / dynamic nodes | Native |

## Failure modes

- **Zero-index hang**: If `0` enters `i += i & -i`, `0 & 0 == 0` loops indefinitely. Always shift to 1-based indexing at the wrapper boundary.
- **Integer overflow in dual-BIT range updates**: Range-add/range-sum uses `i * B1.sum(i) - B2.sum(i)`. Even if `B1` sums fit in 32 bits, multiplying by `i` up to `10^6` overflows `int32`.
- **Applying subtraction to non-groups**: Attempting range-XOR works (XOR is its own inverse), but attempting range-OR or range-max fails silently when subtracting `prefix(l - 1)`.
- **Lock-free read/write races**: Readers and writers traverse opposite directions (`-=` vs `+=`), so concurrent mutation without synchronization produces non-linearizable prefix sums.

## High-throughput and multi-dimensional extensions

In 2D grids (e.g., spatial heatmaps or image integral tables), nesting `i += i & -i` and `j += j & -j` yields O(log R * log C) updates and queries over an `(R+1) x (C+1)` matrix, though memory grows quadratically (`O(R * C)`). For sparse 2D spaces, replacing inner rows with compressed-coordinate 1D BITs or `std::unordered_map` trades cache locality for memory.

In high-frequency analytics, Fenwick Trees can also be vectorized: for small `N <= 1024`, a flat SIMD prefix scan can outperform O(log N) branchy loops, whereas for `N >= 10^5`, the `log2(N)` cache-line touches of a Fenwick Tree dominate.

## Practical checklist

- Allocate `N + 1` elements of `int64` / `double` (with caution for float cancellation) and keep index `0` unused.
- Verify the monoid has an exact inverse (`+`/`-`, `^`/`^`) before selecting a Fenwick Tree over a Segment Tree.
- Use the single-pass `parent = i + (i & -i)` loop for O(N) initialization on static datasets.
- Implement `lowerBound(k)` via top-down binary lifting instead of wrapping `prefixSum` inside binary search.
- Coordinate-compress sparse keys upfront or guard against dynamic key insertions exceeding `N`.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Fenwick Tree Prefix Sums

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A 1-indexed array that maintains dynamic prefix sums and point updates in O(log N) time using two's complement bit isolation (`i & -i`), requiring zero pointer overhead and half the memory of a segment tree.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Flat Primitive Array applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Binary Lifting Cursor.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Binary Lifting Cursor experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce strict 1-based indexing at the public API boundary (`idx + 1` internally) and assert `i >= 1` before entering bit-manipulation loops.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: When you need fast cumulative sums over a mutable array, isolating the lowest set bit with `i & -i` lets a flat array act as an implicit binary tree in L1/L2 cache.
Avoid trap: Allocating `new long[N]` instead of `new long[N + 1]`, triggering an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` when updating index `N`.
Avoid trap: Using `rangeSum(l, r) = sum(r) - sum(l)` instead of `sum(r) - sum(l - 1)`, which drops the element at index `l`.
When to reach for it: You maintain a fixed-size mutable frequency or weight array of size N where both point updates and prefix/range sum queries occur at high frequency (e.g., >100k ops/sec).
When to reach for it: Memory footprint and CPU cache locality are critical—a Fenwick Tree stores N+1 primitives (e.g., 512 KB for 65,536 `int64` entries) versus 2N–4N nodes for a segment tree.

putItTogether.title: Putting Fenwick Tree Prefix Sums Together
putItTogether.summary: When you need fast cumulative sums over a mutable array, isolating the lowest set bit with `i & -i` lets a flat array act as an implicit binary tree in L1/L2 cache.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Fenwick Tree Prefix Sums before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Storing `int64` volumes in a 512 KB Fenwick Tree fits comfortably in L2 cache. Point updates and range depth queries each execute at most 16 loop iterations (~35–50 ns in C++/Rust), avoiding pointer chasing and GC pressure.
